N0.r: *Penzer II 232 n., VII 72 n. 2; Paton Encyc. Rel. and Ethics s.v. “Gambling”; *Fb “kort” II 278; Jewish: *Neuman.
N0.p: A general heading for wagers and gambling in folk tales.

N1.r: Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 70—73, 210; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman.
N1.p: A general heading for characters who are gamblers.

N1.0.1.p: A person gambles because evil demons have taken possession of them.

N1.1.p: A hero becomes wealthy by winning money through gambling.

N1.2.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 354 n. 276, (Zuñi): Benedict II 342, (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 5.
N1.2.p: A gambler who has lost everything is given supernatural power and so wins back his fortune.

N1.2.1.p: A broken die miraculously changes the outcome of a game of chance, saving a man from ruin.

N1.2.2.p: Gambling dice are made from bones taken from a graveyard.

N1.3.p: Two kings make a wager against each other, each betting on the outcome of a contest.

N2.p: Something wagered in a game of chance is unusually large or valuable.

N2.0.1.p: A gambler agrees to play for a stake whose exact nature is left unspecified, so the prize is open-ended and can be named later.

N2.0.2.p: The winner of a game does not take the agreed stakes, and instead insists on playing another game.

N2.1.r: Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 882; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 354 n. 277.
N2.1.p: A person bets his own body as the stake, and if he loses he becomes the winner's slave.

N2.2.r: *Fb “spille” III 487b; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Burmese: Scott Indo-Chinese 323; Hawaii Beckwith Myth 111, 459; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 354 n. 277; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 71 No. 15.
N2.2.p: A character gambles with his own life or the lives of others as the stake.

N2.3.p: A character puts parts of his body up as a stake in a game.

N2.3.1.p: A character wagers his own head as the stake in a game.

N2.3.2.r: To be cut off. Penzer II 232n.
N2.3.2.p: A character wagers one of his hands as the stake in a game.

N2.3.2.1.p: A character wagers both hands and both feet as the stake in a game.

N2.3.3.r: *Type 613; Christiansen FFC XXIV 48ff., 55; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 82.
N2.3.3.p: A character wagers his eyes as the stake in a game.

N2.3.4.p: A character wagers his nose as the stake in a game.

N2.3.5.p: A character wagers his intestines as the stake in a game.

N2.4.p: Helpful animals are lost when their owner gambles them away in a wager.

N2.5.r: *Fb “spille” III 487b, “konge” II 264b; Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 429.
N2.5.p: An entire kingdom or all of a person's property is staked as the wager in a game.

N2.5.1.p: A person loses his right to inherit the throne by gambling it away.

N2.5.2.p: Half of a kingdom is staked as the wager in a game.

N2.6.r: *Fb “spille” III 487b; Irish myth: *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 216 No. 165; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 354 n. 276.
N2.6.p: A character wagers his wife as the stake in a game.

N2.6.1.p: A character wagers his sister as the stake in a game.

N2.6.2.p: A character wagers his daughter as the stake in a game.

N2.6.3.p: A character wagers a young woman as the stake in a game.

N2.7.r: Danish: Grundtvig No. 238; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
N2.7.p: A character wagers his love, or the love of someone, as the stake in a game.

N3.p: A supernatural being, such as a witch or giant, becomes the opponent in a wager or game of chance and is the adversary the hero must face.

N3.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Zuñi) *Benedict II 338.
N3.1.p: A character gambles against a god, with a supernatural being as the opponent in the wager.

N4.r: Fb “kort” II 279a, “klör” II 204; Alphabet No. 450; Scala Celi 110b, 111a Nos. 615, 616; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 33, 36, Beal XXI 311, 313; Missouri French: Carrière.
N4.p: The devil plays games of chance or wagers with a human, so he is portrayed as a gambler.

N4.0.1.p: The devil cheats while playing cards with a human opponent.

N4.1.p: The devil makes a wager with the man who built Cologne Cathedral.

N4.2.p: A person plays a game of chance or skill against a supernatural, non-human being.

N5.r: Type 1839A; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1785E*. Cf. Type 1839B.
N5.p: A parson plays cards all Saturday night, then falls asleep in church and calls out the names of the cards during the service.

N6.p: A person's success at gambling is attributed to good luck, which may come from a supernatural source.

N6.1.r: Scala Celi 24a No. 154; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 55 No. 408A*, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 70—73.
N6.1.p: A gambler gets good luck at games because he has made a compact with the devil.

N6.2.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 81.
N6.2.p: A man loses his luck in gambling because his wife is unfaithful to him, deceived so that he will lose.

N6.3.p: A saint helps a gambler win.

N7.p: A rat, or a trained or transformed rat, upsets the game pieces during a gambling game, and a trained or transformed cat chases it away.

N8.p: A gambler is distracted from his game by women, causing him to lose attention and perhaps the wager.

N9.p: A miscellaneous motif about wagers and gambling that does not fit the more specific categories in this group.

N9.1.p: A gambler loses all of his possessions in play.

N10.p: A person bets on the behavior of a wife, husband, or servant, to see whether that person will do as the other demands.

N11.r: Type 1415; *BP II 199; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 187 n. 131.
N11.p: A husband bets on his wife's complacency: though he has foolishly gambled away everything, she praises him, and he wins the wager.

N12.r: *Type 901; *Wesselski Märchen 216 No. 24; von der Hagen I lxxxii; *Köhler-Bolte I 137; Shakespeare’s “The Taming of the Shrew”; N. A. Indian (Zuñi): Boas JAFL XXXV 76.
N12.p: A husband tames his shrewish wife so that he wins a wager that she will be the most obedient.

N12.1.p: A merchant wagers that a raja's daughter will bring a servant's dinner out into the field, not knowing that she is his wife.

N13.r: One is told to drown himself: loses wager. England: Baughman.
N13.p: Husbands wager that they will be able to make their wives do what they tell them to do.

N15.r: *Type 882; *Köhler-Bolte I 211f., 375, 581; **G. Paris Romania XXXII 481ff.; *von der Hagen III lxxxiii; Boccaccio Decameron II No. 9 (Lee 42); Shakespeare’s “Cymbeline”; *Child V 500 s.v. “wager”.—Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 110; England: Baughman; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 276ff., III 109, 304; India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 62, 253ff.
N15.p: A man bets that his wife cannot be seduced. Other men try and fail to seduce her, and false evidence is offered against her, but the husband still wins the wager.

N15.1.p: A chastity wager in which the woman does give in to seduction, so the husband loses the bet.

N15.2.p: A wager that a nun will remain chaste, placed on her virtue and resolved by whether she keeps it.

N16.p: Wagers made about children who have not yet been born.

N16.1.p: A bet on whether an unborn child will be a boy or a girl.

N16.2.p: Fathers whose yet-unborn children are promised in marriage bet on which of them will rule the household.

N25.r: *Type 889; Wesselski Märchen 200; Wesselski Mönchslatein I No. 1; Fb “lyve” II 491a, “sandhed” III 157b; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
N25.p: A master bets that his servant is honest. A neighbor's wife seduces the drunken servant, but the servant confesses everything to his master, who wins the wager.

N50.p: A general heading for wagers not covered by the more specific categories.

N51.r: *Type 7; Dh I 193; Krohn Bär (Wolf) und Fuchs (JSFO VI) 65ff.; Fb “træ” III 867b; N. A. Indian (San Carlos Apache): cf. Goddard PaAM XXIV 24.
N51.p: A contest in which each side must name three kinds of trees first. The bear names different varieties of the same tree, so the fox wins.

N51.1.p: A wager about tree names in which the learned, scholarly names given by a Brahmin are contrasted with the common names known to a servant, which illiterate peasants confirm.

N53.p: A man bets that a day is lucky, and keeps insisting he is right even after many misfortunes.

N55.p: A contest in which people bet on who is the better shot with a gun or bow.

N55.1.p: The loser of a shooting bet must go naked into thorny bushes to get a bird that was shot.

N56.p: A woman bets she can do a somersault in the middle of the public square. She lands slightly off-center and so loses.

N61.r: *Type 613; *BP II 468ff.; **Christiansen FFC XXIV 47; Chauvin V 11 No. 8, 13 No. 9, 14 No. 158; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 489; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 395.
N61.p: A wager that falsehood is better than truth, decided by an unjust judge who lets the lie win.

N63.p: A trickster pretends to have a toothache and asks for remedies from everyone, recording each helper as a doctor, and so wins a bet that there are more doctors than men of other trades.

N66.r: Test: money given to workman is stolen or lost; lead for his work given him is lent to fisherman who rewards him with a fish in which is a diamond. *Chauvin VI 32 No. 202.
N66.p: A wager over whether wealth is better earned from invested capital or from working at a trade.

N67.p: A trickster bets that women can be made to give alms. He announces that only women who have deceived their husbands are exempt, so the women give to avoid admitting it.

N71.p: A bet that a preacher can begin a sermon with an illustration drawn from card-playing; the card-playing parson wins.

N72.p: A king is persuaded to bet heavily that a second marvelous object will also be ordinary, after the first marvel has turned out to be ordinary.

N73.p: A wager on whether a man or an animal is harder to satisfy with food. Nuts scattered before a master's well-fed guests are snatched and eaten by the guests, and the herdsman wins the bet.

N75.p: A wager that someone can swallow an egg in one gulp. Tricksters give a fool an egg with a chick inside; when he hears the chick peep as he starts to swallow, he claims the chick peeped too late and so wins the bet.

N77.p: A wager in which a bullock is pitted against an elephant. The elephant is frightened and runs away, so the bullock wins.

N78.p: A wager with a ghoul or ogre, which is won by the human side.

N90.p: A general heading for miscellaneous wagers and gambling stories that do not fit the more specific categories.

N91.p: Someone buys a sealed box without knowing what is inside it, gambling on its contents.

N92.p: A bet that is won or lost depending on whether a jackal howls or a donkey brays before the game ends.

N94.p: A father hides his wealth so that his son cannot gamble it away.

N100.r: Penzer V 182f.; *Köhler Aufsätze 99ff.; *Patch Fortuna 78; Irish myth: Cross.
N100.p: A general heading for stories about the nature of luck and fate and how they work.

N101.r: *Cosquin Contes Indiens 126f.; Hdwb. d. Märchens II 63 s.v. Fatalismus; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N101.p: Fate is unavoidable; no one can escape what is destined for them.

N101.1.p: Fate is unavoidable and sorrow comes to everyone. A king who has decreed that no sorrow may fall on a certain day is blinded by a swallow while he sleeps.

N101.2.p: Fate brings death to someone who breaks a taboo.

N101.3.p: A man cannot die: a snake will not bite him even when he provokes it.

N101.4.p: A man who is fated to become king does so even though he breaks the tooth in which his luck was kept.

N102.p: Good fortune comes to both those who deserve it and those who do not.

N110.p: A general heading where luck and fate are imagined as a person or being.

N111.r: **Patch Fortuna; *Penzer I 106f., 135, II 49, 116, III 24, 74, 298, VI 42, 72, 105 n. 1, 124, 156, 159, VII 70, VIII 87; Frazer Pausanias III 424; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N111.p: Luck or fate imagined as a goddess named Fortuna.

N111.1.p: Fortuna, the personified goddess of luck, has a dwelling place.

N111.1.1.p: Fortuna's home is in another world beyond ordinary life.

N111.1.2.p: Fortuna's home is on an island in the otherworld.

N111.2.p: A description of how Fortuna appears to people.

N111.2.1.p: Fortune, personified as a goddess, is depicted as blind.

N111.2.1.1.p: Fortune is shown with a single eye, and that one eye watches over everyone.

N111.2.2.p: Fortune is depicted with two faces.

N111.2.3.p: Fortune is depicted as half white and half black, showing good and bad luck together.

N111.3.r: ; *Köhler-Bolte II 66; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 122, Beal XXI 336; Jewish: *Neuman.
N111.3.p: Fortune is pictured as a wheel that turns, raising some people up and bringing others down.

N111.3.1.p: A dead king inside a mountain is the one who turns Fortune's wheel.

N111.3.2.p: Fortune holds a pair of scales in his hands and weighs each man's balance of good and bad luck.

N111.4.p: Stories about how Fortune deals with human beings and treats them, for good or ill.

N111.4.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 81 (ET 470), 125 (ST 341); Halm Aesop No. 316; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
N111.4.1.p: A man thanks the earth for saving his life, and says that if he had fallen into a well he would have blamed Fortune instead.

N111.5.p: A giant serves as a clerk to the God of Destiny and measures out the lifespan of each mortal.

N112.p: Bad luck is imagined as a person or being with its own identity.

N112.1.p: Bad luck is captured and shut inside a sack, so that the person is rid of it.

N113.p: Good luck is imagined as a person or being with its own identity.

N113.1.p: Good fortune is located in a physical object that carries it.

N113.1.1.p: Zeus gives men a casket containing Good Luck.

N113.2.p: The personification of Good Luck lives in a person's forehead.

N113.2.1.p: A person's right hand is considered lucky, bringing good fortune.

N113.2.2.p: A man's luck is kept in one of his teeth.

N113.3.p: The personification of Good Luck leaves a palace because the king is fated to die that night.

N113.4.p: A certain place is where good luck can be found.

N114.p: Luck or fortune is imagined as an old woman who decides how good or bad a person's fortune will be.

N115.p: Fate is pictured as a book in which the destiny of each person is written down in advance.

N118.p: A person leaves a decision or outcome to luck or chance rather than choosing deliberately.

N118.1.p: A ship is left without a steering course, letting the winds carry it wherever fate wishes.

N119.p: Miscellaneous tales in which luck or fate is personified or appears as a figure.

N119.1.p: A dog tries to catch its own fate by biting at its tail.

N119.2.p: A buffalo's fate is found in a bamboo plant growing out of its head.

N119.3.p: A king's face is ill-omened and foretells evil; his appearance is a sign of coming misfortune. Found in India (Thompson-Balys).

N120.p: Ways in which luck or fate is determined or fixed for a person.

N121.p: A person's fate is settled already before they are born.

N121.1.p: A child is born with objects that show what its fate will be.

N121.1.1.r: Type 934*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 934C*; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI No. 934I.
N121.1.1.p: The spirit of a newborn child appears in uniform, showing its fate; God has determined the fates of everyone.

N121.1.2.p: A newborn child is born holding a weapon and a game animal, which shows it is fated to become a hunter.

N121.2.r: BP III 472ff.; Irish: Beal XXI 336, O’Suilleabhain 120.
N121.2.p: A mother is shown the evil fates her children would have had, and so finds that death spared them from those fates.

N121.3.p: A newborn girl is fated to become a courtesan, a prostitute or mistress.

N121.4.r: (Cf. Z71.5.) Argentina: Jijena Sanchez 54, 64; Spain: ibid. 69; Portugal: ibid. 70.
N121.4.p: A seventh daughter is predestined to become a magician or sorceress.

N122.p: Certain places are regarded as lucky or unlucky, and this determines a person's fortune.

N122.0.1.p: At a place where three roads meet, an ambiguous inscription says what will happen on each road; brothers each pick a different road and their fates follow.

N122.1.p: Certain places are considered unlucky, so that bad fortune is believed to befall those who go there.

N125.p: A choice or outcome is made by chance rather than by deliberate selection.

N125.1.p: The person on whom a feather or wisp falls is chosen to become the king's fool.

N125.2.p: A person's luck depends on whether a demigod with a crooked neck is looking at them.

N125.3.p: A king will stay victorious only as long as he rides a gelding that has been muzzled.

N125.4.p: Districts or regions get their names from the first person encountered in each one.

N126.p: Lots are drawn or cast to decide what luck or fate will bring.

N126.1.p: Lots are cast to decide who will set out on an adventure or quest.

N126.2.p: Lots are cast to decide who is the father of an illegitimate child.

N127.p: A particular day is considered lucky, so it is favored for undertakings.

N127.0.1.p: People born on different days of the week have different kinds of luck.

N127.1.p: Tuesday is regarded as a lucky day.

N127.2.p: Wednesday is regarded as a lucky day, or sometimes as an unlucky one.

N127.3.p: Thursday is regarded as a lucky day.

N127.4.p: Friday is regarded as a lucky day.

N128.p: Certain days are considered unlucky, often called cross-days, and are avoided.

N128.0.1.p: Certain tragic deaths are said to have occurred on particular days of the week.

N128.1.p: National disasters always happen on the same calendar date.

N128.2.p: Monday and Wednesday are regarded as unlucky days.

N130.p: A person's luck or fate can be changed.

N131.p: Actions are performed deliberately in order to change one's luck.

N131.1.p: Luck changes for the better after sexual intercourse.

N131.2.p: Turning to the right, in a certain place, brings good luck.

N131.3.p: Spilling salt is believed to bring bad luck to the person who spills it.

N131.3.1.p: In a story, Judas Iscariot knocks over salt at the Last Supper, explaining why spilled salt is unlucky.

N131.4.p: A person's luck changes after they take a new name.

N131.5.p: A person's luck changes after they move to a new place.

N134.p: Certain people are able to bring about a change in someone's luck, for good or ill.

N134.1.p: Certain people bring bad luck to those around them.

N134.1.1.p: It is unlucky to have a man in the house while cloth is being dyed.

N134.1.2.p: A wife brings bad luck to her husband's family.

N134.1.3.p: People lose their luck as a punishment.

N134.1.4.p: A spirit of misfortune brings bad luck to a house.

N134.1.5.p: A passenger brings bad luck to a ship.

N135.p: Certain objects bring a change in luck, for good or ill.

N135.1.r: **Böklen Die “unglückezahl” Dreizehn (Leipzig, 1913); Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Zahlen” B 13; *Fb “tretten”; **Kyriakiodos To Dysoionon tou Arithmou 13 (Athens, 1953).
N135.1.p: The number thirteen is considered unlucky.

N135.2.r: Nothing escapes a mouse as long as she has in her hole a purse of money Chauvin II 94 No. 45; Bødker Exempler 291 No. 49.
N135.2.p: Having money brings luck to the person who has it.

N135.2.1.p: Finding a hidden hoard of treasure brings good luck.

N135.3.r: *Type 844; **Köhler Aufsätze 119ff.; H. C. Andersen’s “Lykkens Galocher”; Edwin Markham’s “The Shoes of Fortune.”
N135.3.p: A king is told he will become lucky if he wears the shirt of a lucky man, but the only man who claims to be lucky has no shirt.

N135.3.1.r: No one comes. *Köhler-Bolte I 579; Köhler Aufsätze 130.
N135.3.1.p: A feast is to be held for those who have never known sorrow, as ordered in Alexander's dying letter to his mother.

N135.4.p: Certain marks on the body are believed to bring good luck.

N136.p: A judge's boots bring bad luck: a wealthy merchant who acquires them through exchange or theft becomes a beggar.

N137.p: A wise man, a philosopher, overcomes an unfavorable fate.

N140.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about the nature of luck and fate, collected under this category rather than describing a single event.

N141.r: *Type 945; BP III 53f.; Tille FFC XXXIV 254; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 IV 47, 128, 276, 281; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N141.p: A dispute over whether luck or cleverness is the stronger force: a clever man stays poor and is brought to court, and is saved only by pure luck.

N141.1.p: People argue over whether learning or wit is more important.

N141.2.p: People argue over whether wealth or wisdom is the more powerful.

N141.3.p: A contest over which is more beautiful, the nymph of good luck or the nymph of ill luck, with good luck seen as arriving and ill luck as departing.

N141.4.p: Wealth marries a weaver to a princess to prove to Wisdom that the weaver is the more powerful of the two.

N142.r: Chauvin II 109 No. 72; Bødker Exempler 305 No. 76; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
N142.p: Destiny is shown to be worth more than work, outward show, or speculation: a peasant earns a little by labor, a nobleman more by display, a merchant still more by speculation, and a prince most of all by his destiny.

N143.p: Luck only favors money that has been earned honestly; wealth gained dishonestly does not bring good fortune.

N145.p: A princess who has been cast out nevertheless prospers because good luck is with her.

N146.p: A man who is not fated to die cannot be killed, no matter how he is attacked.

N170.p: A general heading for stories showing that luck is unpredictable and capricious, favoring some people for no clear reason.

N171.p: An unprotected son makes his fortune while a protected son has bad luck.

N172.p: A prodigal, wasteful person is nonetheless favored by fortune.

N172.1.p: A wasteful prodigal son is favored over a loyal, faithful son.

N173.p: An unpleasant, disliked young man is nonetheless favored by fortune.

N174.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 247 No. 58.
N174.p: A careful builder who works outside is killed when a storm comes, while a careless builder is saved.

N177.p: A beggar who is refused hospitality must sleep outdoors and so escapes when the house he was refused shelter in burns down.

N178.p: A man who is to be buried alive with a king is spared because he has lost an eye, which makes him unacceptable for the burial.

N178.1.r: Chauvin II 152 No. 18; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
N178.1.p: A king orders a man killed in a fight, but the man breaks his leg and cannot take part; meanwhile the king learns of his innocence.

N178.2.p: A man is chosen for execution because he is fat.

N178.3.p: A king's counselor is expelled from the court and so escapes going along with the king, who is then killed by robbers. His dismissal turns out to be the means of saving his life.

N178.4.p: Robbers drive off a herd of cattle but leave behind one cow, the only one that is lame or crippled.

N181.p: A rich brother and a poor brother each receive fortune's guidance. Fortune tells the poor man to seek his luck under a bush, and there he is advised to become a merchant, after which he grows rich.

N182.p: A woman dreams of a pot of gold. Robbers overhear, find only a snake in the pot, and put it in her bed; the snake then turns into gold.

N183.r: Type 935**; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 946*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 114 No. 945A*.
N183.p: A sum of money is lost twice and only recovered on the third attempt.

N185.p: A woman fleeing with a baby is spared, while a woman without children is killed instead.

N186.p: A man who mocks another's belief in astrology later becomes a respected astrologer himself.

N187.p: A hero searching for a certain man fails to meet him, even though the two are very close to each other.

N200.p: A general heading for the good gifts or blessings that fortune bestows on people.

N201.r: It so happens. *Type 707; *BP II 380ff., 393; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 388.
N201.p: Girls wish to marry a king, prince, or other exalted man, and the wish is granted.

N202.r: Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 87, 420, II 824.
N202.p: A general heading for wishes for good fortune that come true.

N202.1.p: A wish is granted that every woman will fall in love with a certain man the moment she sees him.

N203.p: A person who is unusually lucky in everything they do.

N211.p: A lost object somehow finds its way back to its owner.

N211.1.r: (Polycrates.) *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 635; *Wesselski Mönchslatein 188 No. 146; *Chauvin V 17 No. 10, 141 No. 68, VI 32 No. 202; Fb “ring” IV 328b; Toldo VIII 40; Saintyves “L’Anneau de Polycrate” Revue de l’histoire des religions (1912) 1—32; *Loomis White Magic 121.—Irish: Plummer clxxxiv, *Cross; Norwegian: Solheim Register 20; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman, *Gaster Exempla 210 No. 118, *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 II 106, 344, III 51, 55, 300; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 29; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 7; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 133.
N211.1.p: A lost ring is later found inside a fish.

N211.1.0.1.p: Lost articles are found inside a fish through the power of a saint.

N211.1.1.p: A lost pin is later found inside a fish.

N211.1.2.p: A key that unlocks fetters is found inside a fish.

N211.1.3.p: A lost sword is later found inside a fish.

N211.1.4.p: A lost trinket is later found inside a fish.

N211.1.5.p: A lost brooch, belonging to a saint, turns up inside a fish, so the object comes back to its owner by chance.

N211.2.p: Someone tries in vain to get rid of their slippers, but they always come back to them.

N211.3.p: An angel helps a person find a lost pin.

N212.r: *Type 745; *Chauvin II 129 No. 137; *Herbert III 234, 377 No. 61, 447; *Oesterley No. 109, Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 934B*; Russian: Andrejev No. 834B*; West Indies: Flowers 563.
N212.p: Money is destined to go to a certain person and cannot be kept away from them; a miser who hides his hoard finds it ends up with the poor man he was warned about.

N212.1.p: A husband's magic gift, passed by his wife to a lover and then sold, ends up returning to him.

N213.p: A man is destined by fate to become rich.

N215.p: A tiger carries off a child, a griffin catches the tiger, a lioness kills the griffin, and the lioness raises the child with her own cubs.

N221.r: Irish: Beal XXI 329, O’Suilleabhain 90; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 45, 52 Nos. 313, 345, Espinosa II Nos. 122ff., 168—171, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 70—73, 210.
N221.p: A man is given the magical ability to always win at cards.

N222.p: Whatever objects a person first picks up on a certain occasion bring them good fortune.

N223.p: A man must have a drinking horn; when he sets off to search for one, he stumbles and discovers that one is already at hand.

N224.p: A man refuses a treasure offered to him as a gift, and later finds that same treasure on his own.

N225.r: Boccaccio Decameron II No. 2 (Lee 25); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
N225.p: A man who has been robbed and left penniless is taken in by a wealthy widow and becomes rich.

N226.r: Boccaccio Decameron II No. 4 (Lee 30); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
N226.p: A shipwrecked man is saved clinging to a chest of jewels and so becomes rich.

N227.r: Marries her. (Cf. N251.3.) Italian Novella: Rotunda.
N227.p: A man who has become poor is given a high position by a princess who is secretly in disguise.

N228.p: A leopard tied in a bag and thrown into water floats ashore and finds a mate, as a reward to the trickster who tied him up.

N231.p: A husband leaves his wife, who has borne fourteen daughters, believing bad luck follows him because he has no son. The daughters find precious stones on the seashore, and the wife becomes prosperous and later finds her husband begging among the poor.

N234.p: A poor youngest son boasts to his older brothers that he will build a palace on a certain spot; by chance he finds treasure there and fulfills his boast.

N250.p: A person suffers continual, repeated bad luck.

N250.1.p: A man who shoots a stork is followed by bad luck.

N250.2.r: Scarcely do they establish themselves in the new home, when bad luck addresses them from the hearth: “I have already waited for you here three days.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 735B*.
N250.2.p: Bad luck persistently pursues a person, and an unlucky couple builds themselves a new home to escape it.

N250.3.p: A god keeps punishing a person, and the person accepts this suffering as the divine will that must be followed.

N250.4.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 735A*; Russian: Andrejev No. 735 I*.
N250.4.p: A poor man gets rid of his bad luck and becomes prosperous. His envious rich brother releases the bad luck, and it then follows the rich brother instead.

N251.r: *Type 938; Herbert III 241; *Oesterley No. 110; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXVIII 154f.; Alphabet No. 311; *Hibbard 3ff.; Boccaccio Decameron II Nos. 6, 8 (Lee 34, 39); *Loomis White Magic 112; **Gerould PMLA XIX 335ff.; Dickson 100 n. 7.—Irish: *Cross; O’Suilleabhain 42, Beal XXI 315; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 374; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 113, 793; West Indies: Flowers 564.
N251.p: A person is hounded by one misfortune after another: goods destroyed, wife abducted by a ship captain, children carried off by animals.

N251.1.p: A man captured by pirates is maimed, crippled and blinded, but he endures it patiently. In the end his dead master's subjects choose him as their ruler.

N251.2.p: A man who wants greater wealth loses everything he has. Just as he is about to be rewarded by the king, the king dies.

N251.3.p: A man who has lost his fortune marries the widow of his rich former master.

N251.4.p: Travelers are pursued by misfortune wherever they go.

N251.5.p: A luckless man becomes successful in everything he does after marrying a lucky woman and living off her luck.

N251.6.p: A wizard father sees a luck-bringing animal at his son's house and orders it killed. His grandchildren eat its meat anyway and become fortunate.

N252.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Greek: Aeschylus Agamemnon line 860; Jewish: Neuman. Cf. story of Job.
N252.p: Messengers arrive one after another to report a series of misfortunes.

N252.1.p: As a warrior sets out for war, messengers tell him that his father, mother, brother and sister have died. He refuses to turn back.

N253.r: *Type 947; *BP III 289f.; Bødker Exempler 277 No. 18; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
N253.p: A man who has survived many misfortunes seems finally safe standing in the shadow of a wall, but the wall falls on him.

N255.p: A person escapes one misfortune only to fall into a worse one.

N255.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *49, 55 (ET 86, 152), 116, 136 (ST 261, 417); Halm Aesop No. 129, 252.
N255.1.p: A stag escapes from hunters but is then eaten by a lion.

N255.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 77 (ET 435), 109 (ST 214, 390); Halm Aesop No. 329.
N255.2.p: A donkey passes from one master to worse masters. Finally the farmer beats him to within an inch of his life and will not spare his hide even after he is dead.

N255.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI *63 (ET 266), 140 (ST 4623; Halm Aesop No. 29.
N255.3.p: A halcyon (kingfisher) builds its nest on a sea cliff to escape hazards on land, but a storm blows the nest away.

N255.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI *83 (ET 499), 116 (ST 260); Halm Aesop No. 121.
N255.4.p: A runaway slave takes refuge in a mill, where he has to work harder than ever.

N255.5.r: Starves. Wienert FFC LVI 63 (ET 265), 116 (ST 259); Halm Aesop No. 202.
N255.5.p: A jackdaw (daw) escaping from captivity gets caught in trees when a thread tied around its foot snags on branches.

N255.6.p: An old man burns himself with gunpowder, then burns himself far worse by pouring hot water over the burn.

N256.p: A general motif for bad luck that clings to certain kinds of people or occupations, so that they keep running into misfortune.

N256.1.p: Goldsmiths are regarded as unlucky people who bring misfortune on themselves or others.

N258.p: A chain of disasters follows from losing a single horseshoe nail, and the master keeps trying to carry on despite each new loss.

N261.r: *Type 248; *BP I 515; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 254 No. 34.
N261.p: A man kills a sparrow's friend, a dog, and the sparrow takes revenge, costing the man first his horse, then his property, and finally his life.

N261.1.p: Seven brothers suffer a long run of misfortunes because they destroyed a bird's nest.

N264.p: A man begs all day or only for an hour, but in either case receives just a small basket of grain, showing that his luck is fixed regardless of effort.

N265.p: A person whose presence brings misfortune to everyone around them.

N265.1.p: A girl whose contact with anyone brings them bad luck and death.

N270.r: Irish: Beal XXI 336, O’Suilleabhain 119; India: Thompson-Balys.
N270.p: A general motif that crimes always end up being discovered sooner or later.

N271.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr Nos. 202—209; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N271.p: A murder is revealed despite the murderer's efforts to hide it.

N271.1.r: *Type 960; *BP II 531; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 98b, *Zachariae Kleine Schriften 134; *Basset 1001 Contes II 381.
N271.1.p: The murderer, seeing the sun's rays, unconsciously repeats the dying man's last words and so gives away the crime.

N271.1.1.p: Moonlight rather than sunlight reveals the murder, as the murderer betrays himself under its light.

N271.2.r: BP II 336, 535; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 116 No. 960.
N271.2.p: A dying man names his sons with unusual names such as "O God" and "O King," which piques the king's curiosity and leads to the murder being discovered.

N271.3.r: *BP II 532; *Amalfi Zs. f. Vksk. VI 115ff.; *Zachariae ibid. IX 336; Scala Celi 100b No. 539; Hertz Abhandlungen 334; Köhler-Bolte II 563; Chauvin II 123, VII 146; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 27.—England: Baughman; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 209; Jewish: *Neuman.
N271.3.p: A murdered man calls on cranes, the only witnesses, to avenge him, and they follow and point out the murderer.

N271.3.1.p: Ravens chase a murderer who has killed two children, leading to his exposure.

N271.4.p: A murder is uncovered because someone understands the speech of birds, and the birds point out the crime.

N271.5.p: A murderer is suspected of theft because of a miracle, and in the course of that inquiry the murder comes to light.

N271.6.p: A child inadvertently reveals a murder.

N271.6.1.r: Africa (Bantu): Torrend Specimens of Bantu Folk-lore from Northern Rhodesia (New York, 1921) 9ff. No. 1, 14ff. No. 2.
N271.6.1.p: A child's song gives away the murder.

N271.7.r: House burns. Diggers discover body. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
N271.7.p: A murder is discovered when workers digging the foundations of a house unearth the victim's body.

N271.8.p: A murderer is discovered because the victim's ring is found and traced back to him.

N271.9.p: A tree follows or reveals the murderer, pointing to the guilty person.

N271.10.p: A ship will not sail or will sink while the murderer is on board.

N271.11.p: Murderers, drunk and quarrelling, end up revealing their crime to others.

N275.p: A criminal confesses because he wrongly believes he has been accused or found out.

N275.1.p: A criminal confesses because he misinterprets the cries of animals as accusing him.

N275.2.p: A criminal confesses because he misunderstands a word in a dialect, thinking he has been accused. His guilt comes to light through the confusion.

N275.3.p: A criminal is exposed by an accidental remark that someone, such as a wife, misunderstands and reacts to by confessing.

N275.4.p: A thief, seeing people in the street laughing or talking, imagines they are mocking him and confesses.

N275.5.p: A criminal present in church takes the words of the service as an accusation and confesses.

N275.5.1.p: A sheep thief confesses when the preacher reads the line "All we like sheep have gone astray," which he takes as a charge against himself.

N277.p: Oxen carry a dead usurer to the gallows to be buried, and then are allowed to go wherever they wish.

N278.p: A supernatural voice reveals and points out the criminal.

N300.p: A general heading for stories in which people suffer misfortunes through accidents rather than deliberate action.

N310.p: A general heading for stories in which people are separated from one another by accident.

N311.r: *M. Bloomfield in Penzer VII xxiv ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N311.p: People become separated from each other while searching for water.

N312.p: Twins are separated when a wild animal carries one of them off.

N313.p: A child follows a bird away and becomes lost from its mother.

N314.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 76.
N314.p: People fall asleep on a rock, which then magically rises upward, carrying them away from others.

N315.p: People become separated because they are on opposite banks of a stream.

N316.p: People become separated from one another while lost in a jungle or forest.

N317.p: A family is torn apart when a shipwreck scatters its members, so they lose one another.

N318.p: Lovers are parted by a chance accident rather than by any choice of their own.

N318.1.p: A man mistakes his sweetheart chasing him for an enemy, so he runs away from her and they are separated.

N318.2.p: A princess runs off and marries the wrong man by accident, having meant to elope with someone else.

N320.p: A person is killed by accident, without the killer knowing who they were.

N320.1.p: A man causes the death of his own daughter without realizing who she is.

N321.r: (Cf. N338.3.) Type 939*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 939*; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI No. 9391.
N321.p: A son comes home after a long absence and is accidentally killed by his own parents, who do not recognize him.

N322.r: Icelandic: *Boberg. Cf. death of Polonius in Shakespeare’s “Hamlet”.
N322.p: Someone who is secretly listening in is accidentally killed by another person who does not know they are there.

N322.1.p: A man disguised as the devil is listening in and is accidentally killed by his daughter's lover, who thinks he is a real devil.

N322.2.p: A wife hides in the bushes to eavesdrop and is accidentally killed by her husband, who does not know she is there.

N323.r: *Type 931; *Krappe Balor 13 n. 45; Greek: *Grote I 206; India: Thompson-Balys. See all references to M343 (Parricide prophecy).
N323.p: A prophecy that someone will kill their parent comes true, though the person does it unknowingly.

N324.p: A man kills a prince by accident without knowing who he is.

N324.1.p: A prince who has been transformed into an animal or other form is accidentally killed without anyone recognizing him.

N325.p: A person is killed by someone who, in a state of madness, has a false belief that makes them act without knowing what they are doing.

N325.1.p: A man, believing he is cutting a branch, actually kills his own son.

N325.2.p: Women driven mad eat the flesh of their own infants.

N325.3.p: A mother, believing her son is a wild beast, kills him.

N330.p: A death or killing happens by accident, with no one intending it.

N331.p: Objects accidentally fall and strike a person, killing them.

N331.1.p: A dagger hanging in the wall above a bed falls and kills a girl. Her lover had secretly placed it there.

N331.1.1.p: A knife accidentally falls from the wall and strikes a girl's throat, killing her.

N331.1.2.p: A prince's arrow accidentally grazes the breast of a merchant's wife.

N331.1.3.p: A bride accidentally lets a dagger fall, and it kills her husband.

N331.2.p: A piece of bread dropped from a tree lands on a bear's nose and kills it.

N331.2.1.p: A man hiding in a tree is so frightened of a lioness that he drops his sword, which accidentally kills her.

N332.p: Someone is accidentally poisoned or poisons another by mistake.

N332.1.r: Type 837; *De Vries Tijdschrift voor Nederlandsche Taal- en Letterkunde XLVII 63ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N332.1.p: A son is accidentally fed bread that his wicked father had poisoned for someone else; a beggar gives the poisoned loaf to the son.

N332.1.1.p: A poisoned bath, prepared for one person, is accidentally used by the hero instead.

N332.2.p: A poisoned cup meant for the hero instead poisons his horse: the hero spurs his horse away, the poison spills into the horse's ear, and the horse dies.

N332.2.1.p: An elephant on a rampage is accidentally poisoned instead of a man, and the man claims to have killed the elephant.

N332.3.r: *Chauvin VIII 60 No. 25; *Krappe Balor 184 n. 12; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas III 96; India: Thompson-Balys.
N332.3.p: A bird carrying a serpent lets its poison drop into a milk supply, so everyone who drinks the milk is poisoned.

N332.3.1.p: The head of a snake that was killed bites and kills a king.

N332.3.2.p: A snake hidden in a jug bites a would-be thief.

N332.4.p: A boy accidentally drinks a poison that was meant for his stepbrother, because the doctor had secretly swapped in a sleeping potion for the requested poison.

N332.4.1.p: A youth accidentally takes the poison he had intended for his father.

N332.5.p: A woman unknowingly poisons her own son, mistaking the poison for medicine.

N332.6.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 177; Jewish: *Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 511.
N332.6.p: A man eats food that has been poisoned by some unexplained means.

N332.7.p: Hidden fruit is accidentally poisoned by a snake.

N333.p: Aiming at a fly leads to someone's death.

N333.1.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 285. Cf. Type 1586.
N333.1.p: A person is killed when someone hits a fly that has landed on his face.

N333.1.1.p: A foolish man slaps a crying child to quiet it and kills the child by the blow.

N333.2.p: A man is accidentally killed by a bear that is trying to drive away flies from him.

N334.p: A game or joke accidentally ends in someone's death.

N334.1.r: *Type 2401; *BP I 202; Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 431; England, U.S.: Baughman.
N334.1.p: Children playing at hog-killing accidentally kill one of their number.

N334.2.r: Wesselski Theorie 18; Fb “hænge” I 731b; Danish: Christensen DF XLVII 200 No. 36; Icelandic: Boberg; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3309, Legends Nos. 605 609; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 122 Nos. 40, 41.
N334.2.p: A hanging staged as a game or joke accidentally causes the death of the person hanged.

N334.3.p: A practical joker asks a doctor to castrate him as a joke, and the doctor insists on performing the operation.

N335.p: Someone dies unexpectedly at the hands of an animal.

N335.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 65 (ET 295), 207 (ST 197); Halm Aesop No. 171; India: Thompson-Balys.
N335.1.p: A bird hunter is killed by an adder at the very moment he shoots at a bird.

N335.2.r: A pregnant woman demands a bath of blood: husband substitutes a bath of red dye. A Garuda bird attracted by the dye carries her off. Penzer I 97; Dunlop-Liebrecht 135.
N335.2.p: A woman covered in blood from a bloodbath is carried off by a bird that mistakes her for meat.

N335.2.1.p: A sick queen lying under red satin is carried off by a bird that thinks she is red meat.

N335.3.p: A man leaning on a bow is killed when ants have gnawed through its string, causing the bow to rebound and cut off his head.

N335.4.r: Africa (Larusa): Fokken “Erzählungen und Märchen der Larusa” ZsKS VII 82ff. No. 1, (Wachaga): Gutmann 87ff. No. 44, (Masai): Fuchs Sagen, Mythen und Sitten der Masai (Jena, 1910) 50ff., (Uganda): Rowling The Tales of Sir Apolo: Uganda Folklore and Proverbs (London, n.d.) 47ff., (Congo): Stanley My Dark Companions and their Strange Stories (New York, 1906) 161ff., Casati Ten Years in Equatoria and the Return with Emin Pasha (New York, 1891) II 45f.
N335.4.p: An animal gnawing a bone causes a splinter to fly off and kill young animals.

N335.5.p: A hound strikes a spot on an animal that is uniquely vulnerable and kills it.

N335.6.p: A chain of animals is accidentally killed one after another.

N335.6.1.p: An animal attacking another is itself killed by a third animal lying in ambush.

N335.7.p: A tortoise falls onto an elephant's back and breaks it.

N336.p: A man dreams that he is dodging a blow, and in waking he hits his head against a wall and kills himself.

N337.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 63 n. 2; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 715; Africa (Fang): Tessman 135, (Congo): Grenfell 820.
N337.p: Someone is accidentally killed by a weapon that was aimed or thrown in the wrong direction.

N337.1.p: A blind poet accidentally kills his friend.

N337.2.p: A hero measuring a wild boar is mortally wounded by a bristle that accidentally pierces him.

N337.3.p: A man throws an axe at one animal, misses it, and the axe instead kills a different animal.

N338.p: A person is killed by mistake because someone else was taken for them, so the wrong person dies.

N338.1.p: A saint swaps places with a charioteer, and the charioteer is killed in the saint's stead.

N338.2.p: A foolish person dressed up as a king, or taken for one, is killed in the king's place.

N338.3.r: (Cf. N321.) Icelandic: Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda (N366); Greek: Grote I 242; Jewish: Neuman; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 98.
N338.3.p: A son is killed because he is mistaken for someone else.

N338.3.1.p: A father, not recognizing his son, orders him thrown into the sea.

N339.p: A miscellaneous death that happens by accident, not fitting the other categories of accidental death.

N339.1.r: Chases a mouse. Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 310 n. 2.
N339.1.p: A man falls into a jar of honey and drowns in it.

N339.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 61 (ET 242), 146 (ST 512); Halm Aesop No. 293.
N339.2.p: Flies get stuck in honey and die, the death being caused by their greed for the sweetness.

N339.3.p: Foxes crowd into a house and are suffocated by the crush.

N339.4.p: A bridegroom is struck and killed by lightning on his wedding night.

N339.5.p: A king who loved his wife too much is burned to death while taking an alcohol bath.

N339.6.p: A man forgets to put on a magic gown that protects him, and as a result he is killed.

N339.7.p: An army is drowned when an incoming tide rises without the soldiers noticing it.

N339.8.p: A person accidentally dies after falling onto his own weapon, such as a shield.

N339.8.1.p: A father accidentally dies after falling into the fire while taking down weapons for his son.

N339.9.p: A fairy abducts a girl, then leaves her on the shore, where she is accidentally drowned.

N339.10.p: A youth gazing at his own reflection in water falls in and drowns.

N339.11.p: A girl lowers her sari for a hero to climb up, but when he is halfway up the sari tears and he falls to his death.

N339.12.p: A prefect cursed by a bishop dies when a fish bone lodges in his throat.

N339.13.p: A person dies by accidentally hitting their head against the top of a doorway (the lintel).

N339.14.p: A wife, following custom by throwing her dead husband's body into a river, is pulled under and drowned when the corpse's arm catches her.

N339.15.p: A thief is crushed to death when the parts of a wall he has tunneled through collapse on him.

N339.16.p: A king is fatally wounded by poison or infection from the tooth of an enemy he had killed.

N339.17.p: A jinn (spirit) imprisoned in a bottle is accidentally released, and it escapes and kills the person who trapped it.

N340.p: Someone is killed or condemned too quickly, through a mistake, without proper inquiry.

N340.1.p: A person kills themselves out of remorse after having hastily condemned someone who turns out to be innocent.

N340.2.p: A king in haste has seven thousand people executed after they stone his judges to death.

N340.3.p: A woman is wrongly condemned for drunkenness after being seen taking just one drink.

N341.p: A messenger is killed or accused because his message has been misunderstood.

N342.p: A man is hastily condemned because he accidentally appears to be connected with a crime.

N342.1.r: *Type 516; *BP I 42ff.; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 129; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 9; India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 155ff. No. 68.
N342.1.p: A faithful servant who guards his master's wife from danger is falsely condemned as a traitor to his master.

N342.1.1.p: A faithful son who guards his father from a monster is falsely accused by his stepmother.

N342.2.p: A man who stumbles over a bloody corpse and gets blood on himself is accused of murder.

N342.3.r: *Type 303; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 7; India: Thompson-Balys.
N342.3.p: A jealous and overhasty man kills his twin brother, who had just rescued him.

N342.4.p: A false accusation is overheard by someone, who then hastily kills the accused person.

N342.5.p: An angry brother kills his sister's husband, believing he has killed his sister and their baby.

N342.6.p: A woman is wrongly accused of cannibalism after being seen biting off a dead man's finger to get his ring.

N343.r: (Pyramus and Thisbe.) Köhler-Bolte I 4; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Fox 201, **G. Hart Ursprung und Verbreitung der Pyramus und Thisbe-Sage (1889); *C. de Boer Pyramus et Thisbe (Amsterdam, 1911).
N343.p: A lover kills himself, believing his mistress is dead, when she has really only been frightened away by a lion.

N343.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
N343.1.p: A mistress kills herself, believing her lover is dead.

N343.2.1.p: A wife dies believing her husband is dead, and her grief or despair ends her life. The lover in this chain of mistakes kills himself after mistakenly thinking his beloved has died.

N343.3.p: A woman pretends to be dead so she can meet her exiled lover. When he hears of her supposed death, he comes back and gives himself up to be executed, which leads to his death.

N343.4.p: A lover kills himself after finding his beloved dead.

N344.r: (Told also of lovers.) *Schoepperle II 437f.; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 137 n. 4.
N344.p: A father kills himself because he believes his son is dead. The son forgot to raise the white sails that were meant to signal that he was safe.

N344.1.r: *Type 451; BP I 70ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 8.
N344.1.p: Sons are supposed to come home or stay away based on a signal that a sister has been born, but the wrong sign is shown and they leave home.

N344.2.p: A father has his innocent son killed, believing the son has committed adultery with the father's wife.

N345.r: his falcon. When she makes her request it is too late. *Bédier Fabliaux 153f.; Boccaccio Decameron V No. 9 (*Lee 170); Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
N345.p: A poor suitor has only a falcon to hunt with. When his lady's sick son wants the falcon, she comes to ask for it, and the suitor serves the falcon to her as dinner.

N346.r: Chauvin II 104 No. 66; Bødker Exempler 302 No. 69; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
N346.p: A pigeon hastily kills his mate for stealing wheat, but the wheat was only dried out and did not fill the nest. When the dampness later swells the wheat, he realizes his mistake and kills himself in remorse.

N347.p: An innocent man is wrongly suspected of a crime by accident or mistaken identity.

N347.1.r: Scala Celi 59a No. 326; Chauvin IX 19; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Icelandic: Boberg.
N347.1.p: A clerk who goes into a tavern is arrested along with others for a murder.

N347.2.p: A saint who enters a brothel to reform the women is accused of going there with evil intent.

N347.3.p: A boy is hanged for stealing cattle, but the cattle that had only strayed are found later.

N347.4.p: A man buys a stolen ornament without knowing it, then gives it to its owner as a gift. He is thrown into jail as the thief.

N347.5.p: A poor man is given a rich robe by the emperor, and is then locked up as a thief for having it.

N347.6.p: A man who has been falsely accused takes his own life.

N347.7.p: A greedy disciple ignores his learned teacher's warning and stays in the city, and is then condemned to take the place of a thief.

N348.p: A jealous husband kills his innocent wife. Suspicion is aroused when the villain leaves his handkerchief in her room.
